results.note: The single biggest frontend-quality improvement is making the trace-by-cell-click interaction (DataPreview) keyboard- and screen-reader-accessible. Tracing a value is the app's core differentiating debugging feature, yet it is exposed only through a click delegated on a non-interactive table cell with no tabIndex, role, or key handler, so it is completely unreachable without a mouse. Pair that with the systemic missing programmatic labels on node-editor form controls (only 8 of ~146 labels are associated) and a single app-level polite live region wrapping the preview/trace panels, and you would lift the editor from largely screen-reader-opaque to genuinely operable. The codebase already demonstrates the right patterns in NodeSearch (full combobox/listbox), ToggleButtonGroup (radiogroup + roving tabindex), ContextMenu, StepCard, and ModalShell — these fixes are about applying those existing patterns consistently to the data grid, form labels, progress bars, and dynamic-update regions.

findings.title: Preview-table cells (the trace entry point) are keyboard- and screen-reader-inaccessible
findings.description: The core 'click a cell to trace how this value was computed' interaction is implemented as an onClick delegated on <tbody> (line 340) that resolves the target <td data-row-index data-column> (lines 221-234). The cell itself is a plain <td> (DataCell, lines 147-167) with cursor:pointer when clickable but NO tabIndex, NO role="button", and NO onKeyDown. There is no other affordance anywhere to start a trace. Consequently a keyboard-only or screen-reader user cannot reach or activate any cell: the cells are not in the tab order, Enter/Space do nothing, and a screen reader announces them as inert table data with no hint that they are actionable. This makes the application's primary debugging feature (tracing a computed value through the pipeline) entirely mouse-dependent. App.tsx wires handleCellClick into both DataPreview and ExplorePreview (App.tsx:598, 642), so the gap spans every preview surface. The non-clickable column-search input and the trace panel itself are keyboard-reachable, but the bridge between them — selecting a cell — is not.
findings.recommended_fix: Make traceable cells real interactive elements: when onCellClick is provided, render each DataCell with role="button", tabIndex={0}, an aria-label like `Trace ${column} = ${formattedValue}, row ${rowIndex+1}`, and an onKeyDown that fires the same trace on Enter/Space (preventDefault on Space). Keep the existing delegated onClick for mouse users, or move activation onto the cell. For large virtualized grids, a roving-tabindex / grid keyboard model (role="grid" on <table>, role="row"/role="gridcell", arrow-key navigation) is the fuller solution and matches the grid pattern already used in NodeSearch's listbox. Add a test asserting Enter on a focused cell invokes onCellClick with the right (rowIndex, column).

findings.location: frontend/src/panels/editors/* and frontend/src/panels/modelling/* (e.g. GLMTargetConfig.tsx:64-101 selects; ConstantEditor.tsx:31-64 inputs; DataSourceEditor.tsx:94-105 SQL textarea) — ~138 of ~146 <label> elements have no htmlFor and controls have no id/aria-label
findings.title: Node-editor form controls have no programmatic label (visual-only labels, no htmlFor/aria-label)
findings.description: Across the node editors and modelling/optimiser config panels, the pervasive pattern is a visual <label> rendered as a sibling of its <input>/<select>/<textarea> with neither an htmlFor on the label nor an id/aria-label/aria-labelledby on the control. Grep across frontend/src/panels: 146 <label> elements, only 8 use htmlFor (and those 8 are in BandingEditor/RatingStepEditor/GenerateBandsDialog); ~73 form controls in panels/editors alone. Concrete confirmations: GLMTargetConfig.tsx Target/Weight/Offset <select>s (lines 64-101) each have a bare sibling <label> and no id; ConstantEditor.tsx name/value <input>s (lines 41-64) rely only on placeholder; DataSourceEditor.tsx SQL Query <textarea> (lines 98-105) has a sibling un-linked <label>. A screen reader therefore announces these as 'edit text'/'combobox' with no name, and clicking the visible label does not focus the field. This affects the entire GLM/modelling configuration, data-source, constant, scenario-expander, optimiser-apply and sink editors — i.e. essentially all data-entry in the product is unlabelled for assistive tech. (Contrast: ConfigCheckbox.tsx and EditorLabel.tsx already support proper association via useId/htmlFor, and Toolbar's Rows/Chunk inputs correctly use htmlFor — the infrastructure exists but is not applied.)
findings.recommended_fix: Associate every control with its label. Cheapest consistent route: give EditorLabel a required htmlFor and have each editor pass a useId()-generated id that is also set on the control (mirrors the existing ConfigCheckbox pattern). Where a wrapping <label> is acceptable, wrap the control. For toggle/select groups already announced via role, use aria-labelledby pointing at the section label's id. Add an ESLint rule (jsx-a11y/label-has-associated-control) to the frontend eslint config to prevent regression and to surface the full list; gate it in CI.

findings.title: Dynamic preview/trace updates are not announced to screen readers (no live region)
findings.description: The bottom preview panel swaps between 'Executing pipeline...' (DataPreview.tsx:276-279), an error message (281-286 / 416-420), and a results table with 'N rows · M cols' (408-414) purely by re-rendering inert <div>/<span> content. None of these is inside an aria-live region or role="status"/role="alert", and App.tsx renders the whole preview block (584-647) and the TracePanel (677-678) without any live-region wrapper. So a screen-reader user who triggers a preview or a trace gets no notification that execution started, failed, or completed, nor what the new result/trace is — the panel content changes silently. (TracePanel's correlation-diagnostics block does use role="alert" at TracePanel.tsx:126, and LazyNodeEditors wraps the editor suspense fallback in role="status" at line 27, proving the team knows the pattern; it is just absent for the main preview/trace state transitions.)
findings.recommended_fix: Wrap the preview status text in a polite live region: add an off-screen role="status" aria-live="polite" element that announces concise state strings ('Executing pipeline', 'Preview ready: 1,240 rows, 12 columns', 'Preview failed: <error>'). For errors prefer role="alert" (assertive). When a trace opens, either move focus into the TracePanel header (it already has a Close button) or announce 'Trace opened for <column> = <value>' via a live region. Keep announcements short and debounced to avoid chatter on rapid re-previews.

findings.title: Progress indicators have no progressbar semantics (training/optimiser/cache progress invisible to SR)
findings.description: Every progress indicator is a visual-only filled <div>; there is not a single role="progressbar" or aria-valuenow/min/max in the entire frontend (verified by grep). TrainingProgress.tsx (lines 23-28) and the ModellingPreview top bar (lines 92-99) animate width:`${progress*100}%` with no progressbar role and no live region, so screen-reader users get no feedback that a long-running model train is progressing or how far along it is. CacheFetchButton.tsx surfaces progress only as button text ('… rows · Ns', lines 229-234) inside a <button> whose label changes silently (not in a live region). For multi-minute operations (training, optimisation, cache builds) this leaves assistive-tech users unable to tell whether the app is working or hung.
findings.recommended_fix: Add role="progressbar" with aria-valuemin={0} aria-valuemax={100} aria-valuenow={Math.round(progress*100)} and an aria-label (e.g. 'Training progress') to the bar elements in TrainingProgress and ModellingPreview. For indeterminate phases omit aria-valuenow. Mirror the same to OptimiserPreview/OptimiserConfig progress and the cache-build button (announce periodic milestones via a polite live region rather than relabelling the button silently).

findings.location: frontend/src/components/ToggleButtonGroup.tsx:47 (role="radiogroup" aria-label optional); used without ariaLabel in DataSourceEditor.tsx:37, BandingEditor.tsx:351, EdgeJoinEditor.tsx:226, ExternalFileEditor.tsx:33 & :51, ModelScoreEditor.tsx:46, OptimiserApplyEditor.tsx:165, SinkEditor.tsx:62
findings.title: ToggleButtonGroup radiogroups have no accessible name in 8 of 9 usages
findings.description: ToggleButtonGroup renders a role="radiogroup" (line 47) and correctly implements roving tabindex + arrow keys, but its accessible name comes only from the optional ariaLabel/ariaLabelledBy props. Of all production usages, only RatingStepEditor (line 426) passes ariaLabel. The other eight (Source Type, Banding type, EdgeJoin key mode, External file type, External model class, Model score source, Optimiser-apply source, Sink format) render a nameless radiogroup: the visible <label> above the group is a separate un-linked element, so a screen reader announces 'radio group' with no purpose, and the individual radios announce only their own label with no group context. These choices (e.g. flat-file vs Databricks, registered vs experiment-run model) materially change the form, so the missing group name is a real comprehension barrier.
findings.recommended_fix: Pass a meaningful ariaLabel (or ariaLabelledBy referencing the section label's id) at each call site, e.g. ariaLabel="Source type" in DataSourceEditor. Optionally make the prop required in the component's types so new usages must supply a name; an existing test already covers the labelled case.

findings.title: WebSocket/sync error banner is not announced (sibling session-expired banner is)
findings.description: App.tsx renders two top-of-canvas error banners. The sessionExpired banner (lines 518-531) correctly has role="alert" so it is announced. The immediately adjacent syncBanner (lines 533-539) — which carries live-sync/WebSocket failure messages — is a plain <div> with no role="alert"/aria-live, so when the editor loses its connection to the server the message appears silently for screen-reader users. Given this banner communicates that the user's edits may no longer be syncing, missing the announcement is a meaningful reliability/comprehension gap. The banner's dismiss button (line 537) also has no aria-label (its content is a literal glyph that is additionally mojibaked in source: 'âœ•').
findings.recommended_fix: Add role="alert" (or aria-live="assertive") to the syncBanner container so connection-loss messages are announced, matching the sessionExpired banner. Give the dismiss button aria-label="Dismiss" and render the close glyph from a proper icon (lucide X) or an explicit ×, and add aria-hidden to the decorative glyph.

findings.location: frontend/src/components/ColumnTable.tsx:78-87 (checkbox <input> with no accessible name); consumed by ColumnsTab.tsx:129-139 and OutputEditor
findings.title: Column-selection checkboxes have no accessible name
findings.description: ColumnTable renders the output-column selection checkboxes (lines 80-86) as bare <input type="checkbox"> with no id/aria-label/aria-labelledby; the column name lives in a separate <td> (lines 89-96) with no programmatic link. The header cell for the checkbox column is empty (lines 53-56). A screen reader navigating the column picker (ColumnsTab — used to choose which columns a node outputs) therefore hears 'checkbox, not checked' for every row with no indication of which column it controls, making column selection unusable non-visually. Row click toggling works for mouse users (interactiveRows, line 76) but does not help keyboard/SR users identify the target.
findings.recommended_fix: Give each checkbox an accessible name tied to its column, e.g. aria-label={col.name} (or aria-labelledby referencing the name cell's id). Consider rendering the row as a proper label/control association so the visible name is the checkbox's name. Add a header label (visually-hidden) for the checkbox column. A test asserting getByRole('checkbox', { name: col.name }) resolves would lock it in.

findings.location: frontend/src/components/Toast.tsx:30-34 (error toasts never auto-dismiss), :37-38 (role="alert") inside :66 (aria-live="polite" container)
findings.title: Toast live-region politeness conflicts with per-toast role=alert, and persistent error toasts lack a clear close path for SR users
findings.description: ToastContainer wraps all toasts in a region with aria-live="polite" (line 66) while each ToastItem is role="alert" (line 38), which maps to aria-live="assertive". Nesting an assertive alert inside a polite region yields inconsistent/duplicated announcement behaviour across screen readers (the inner role generally wins, but the polite container is then misleading). Separately, error toasts never auto-dismiss (line 31 returns early before the 3s timer), so they persist indefinitely; the only way to clear one is the icon-only X button — which is correctly labelled (aria-label, line 50), so the dismiss itself is reachable, but a persistent assertive alert that stays in the accessibility tree can cause some SRs to re-announce on focus changes. The net effect is noisy/duplicated announcements rather than a hard block.
findings.recommended_fix: Pick one model: drop aria-live from the container and keep role="alert" only on error toasts while using role="status" (polite) for success/info/warning; or keep a single polite container and remove the per-item role. Ensure error toasts are individually dismissible (already true) and consider making the alert non-persistent in the a11y tree after it is read (e.g. move dismissed/long-lived toasts out of the live region).

findings.location: frontend/src/components/Toolbar.tsx:85 (<header role="toolbar">) and :87 (<h1> nested inside the toolbar)
findings.title: Toolbar uses role="toolbar" without arrow-key navigation and nests the only <h1> inside it
findings.description: The top bar is <header role="toolbar"> (line 85). The WAI-ARIA toolbar pattern expects a single tab stop with Left/Right arrow navigation among the controls; here every control (source dropdown, Rows/Chunk inputs, undo/redo, breakdown dropdowns, Utility/Imports/Save/Git) is an independent tab stop and there is no arrow-key roving, so the role advertises an interaction model the component does not implement, which can confuse assistive-tech users. Additionally the document's only <h1> ('Haute', line 87) lives inside this toolbar; combined with dialog <h2>s and a couple of deep <h3>s (RatebookRatesTab, TraceDetail) and no <h2> structuring the main editor regions, the heading outline is essentially flat/non-descriptive for screen-reader document navigation. These are polish-level issues, not hard blockers (all toolbar controls remain individually focusable and labelled).
findings.recommended_fix: Either implement the toolbar roving-tabindex + arrow-key pattern (as ToggleButtonGroup already does) or drop role="toolbar" in favour of a plain <header> with aria-label, since the controls function fine as ordinary sequential tab stops. Move/keep the app <h1> as a real page title and add visually-hidden <h2> landmarks for the canvas/preview/properties regions to give a meaningful heading outline.

results.note: The single biggest frontend-quality improvement is to give NodeSearch (the Ctrl+K command palette) the same modal discipline ModalShell already provides: a focus trap, focus restoration, and aria-modal. It is opened by keyboard, has no Tab trap, and never returns focus on close, so a keyboard-only user who opens it Tabs straight into the canvas/toolbar behind a visually-covering overlay and is left stranded with focus on hidden chrome. More broadly, the codebase has an excellent shared ModalShell (focus trap + restore) but three of its overlay surfaces (NodeSearch, ContextMenu, GenerateBandsDialog) were hand-rolled and each skipped a different piece of that discipline; routing them through (or to the standard of) ModalShell would close every keyboard dead-end in one consistent move.

findings.title: NodeSearch (Ctrl+K palette) has no focus trap and never restores focus on close — keyboard-only dead-end
findings.description: NodeSearch is a full-screen overlay opened primarily by keyboard (Ctrl+K). Unlike the shared ModalShell, it implements its own dialog and provides NONE of: a focus trap, focus restoration, or aria-modal. On mount it focuses the search input (line 83), but pressing Tab from that input moves focus to the next focusable element in DOM order — which is the toolbar/canvas/palette chrome rendered BEHIND the overlay (the backdrop on line 154 is a sibling, and the panel on line 157 is not aria-modal). A keyboard user therefore Tabs straight out of the visually-covering palette into hidden controls with no visible focus context. When the palette closes (Escape, Enter-select, or backdrop click), focus is never returned to the element that was focused before opening (there is no previousFocus capture/restore), so focus silently resets to document.body and keyboard navigation is lost. This is the classic keyboard-only dead-end the project's own ModalShell was built to prevent.
findings.recommended_fix: Render NodeSearch through ModalShell (which already implements focus trap + restore + Escape + aria-modal), or replicate that logic: (1) capture document.activeElement on mount and refocus it in the cleanup; (2) add a Tab handler that wraps focus within the panel (or, given the aria-activedescendant pattern, preventDefault on Tab so focus stays on the input); (3) add aria-modal="true" to the role="dialog" panel on line 158.

findings.title: Invalid listbox/option ARIA structure: focusable <button> elements used as role=option inside a combobox listbox
findings.description: The results container is role="listbox" (line 191) and each result row is a native <button> with role="option" (lines 228-235). The ARIA combobox/listbox pattern in use here keeps DOM focus on the input and drives selection via aria-activedescendant (line 177). Options in that pattern must be non-interactive elements (e.g. <div role="option">); using real <button>s that are themselves in the tab order (buttons are focusable by default) contradicts the activedescendant model and produces an invalid accessible structure (interactive widgets are not allowed as listbox options). Screen readers may double-announce or mis-navigate, and the buttons become extra Tab stops competing with the input's activedescendant model. The off-screen active-row clone (lines 203-221) is correctly a <div role=option>, showing the intended pattern was a non-button option.
findings.recommended_fix: Render each result row as a non-focusable <div role="option"> (with the existing id/aria-selected/aria-posinset/aria-setsize and onClick/onMouseEnter handlers) instead of a <button>, matching the off-screen active clone. Keep all keyboard interaction on the input via the existing handleKeyDown + aria-activedescendant. This removes the spurious Tab stops and makes the listbox structure valid.

findings.location: frontend/src/panels/editors/banding/GenerateBandsDialog.tsx:95-105 (role="dialog" with no Escape handler, no focus management)
findings.title: GenerateBandsDialog declares role="dialog" but has no Escape-to-close, no autofocus, and no focus management
findings.description: GenerateBandsDialog renders role="dialog" / aria-label (lines 96-98) but provides none of the keyboard contract a dialog implies: there is no Escape handler to invoke onClose, no element is auto-focused on open, and there is no focus containment or restoration. (It is an inline elevated card within the banding editor rather than a full overlay, so a hard focus-trap is debatable, but Escape-to-dismiss and initial focus are still expected for anything announced as a dialog.) A keyboard user who opens it must Tab forward through the page to reach its Start field and has no Escape affordance to cancel, while a screen reader announces a 'dialog' that behaves like ordinary inline content. This is inconsistent with the sibling banding GenerateBands/RenameDialog flows that go through ModalShell.
findings.recommended_fix: Add an onKeyDown (or effect-scoped keydown) that calls onClose() on Escape, and focus the first input (e.g. the gen-start field) on mount via a ref/useEffect. If it should behave as a true modal, render it through ModalShell; otherwise drop role="dialog" down to role="group" so the announced semantics match the (non-modal) behaviour.

findings.title: Panel close buttons rely on title="Close" with a bare icon and no aria-label (inconsistent with the rest of the codebase)
findings.description: The shared PanelHeader close button (lines 51-58, used by UtilityPanel, ImportsPanel, GitPanel and any PanelShell-titled panel) and the bespoke NodePanel header close button (lines 907-911) render only a decorative lucide <X/> SVG and provide their accessible name solely via the HTML title attribute — no aria-label. The lucide <X> has no aria-hidden, and title is the lowest-priority source in the accessible-name computation and is announced unreliably across screen readers (and not at all to many keyboard/AT users). This is demonstrably inconsistent with the codebase's own conventions: Toolbar icon buttons (Undo/Redo/Zoom, lines 228/237/279/287), the Toast dismiss (Toast.tsx:50), TracePanel close ("Close trace"), KeyboardShortcuts close, and even the warning-dismiss X in NodePanel.tsx:997 all carry an explicit aria-label. The two most-used panel close affordances are the ones that miss it.
findings.recommended_fix: Add aria-label="Close" (or a more specific label like "Close panel"/"Close node properties") to the PanelHeader close button and the NodePanel header close button, and mark the inner <X> aria-hidden="true". Keeping title for the tooltip is fine, but the accessible name should come from aria-label.

findings.title: Global window Escape/'?' handlers still fire while a dialog is open (no stopPropagation), causing canvas side effects behind modals
findings.description: useKeyboardShortcuts registers its handler on window and treats Escape (lines 143-147 -> clearTrace()+closePanel()) and '?' (lines 150-154 -> toggle shortcuts) as global. Dialogs built on ModalShell (Escape handler at ModalShell.tsx:40-44) and NodeSearch (Escape at lines 142-145) call only e.preventDefault(), never e.stopPropagation(), and listen on document. Because the global handler is on window (the outermost target), pressing Escape inside an open SubmodelDialog/RenameDialog/NodeSearch closes the dialog AND simultaneously runs the canvas's clearTrace()+closePanel(), e.g. silently deselecting the node the user was renaming and clearing any active trace. Pressing '?' is guarded by isTyping for INPUT/TEXTAREA, but the KeyboardShortcuts modal container itself is not an input, so a stray '?' can interact with the global toggle while a different modal is open. The effects are minor today but constitute cross-layer keyboard handling that will surprise users and is brittle as dialogs grow.
findings.recommended_fix: Make modal Escape handlers authoritative when a modal is open: call e.stopPropagation() (and stopImmediatePropagation if needed) in ModalShell and NodeSearch Escape branches, and/or have useKeyboardShortcuts early-return when a modal/dialog is open (e.g. check useUIStore dialog flags, or if document.querySelector('[role=dialog][aria-modal=true]') exists, or if e.target is inside a [role=dialog]). This keeps Escape scoped to the topmost layer.

findings.location: frontend/src/hooks/useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:36-38 (isTyping detection) with Delete/Backspace at 174-191 and Ctrl+A at 122-126
findings.title: Shortcut typing-guard ignores native <select> and contentEditable, so Delete/Ctrl+A can mutate the graph while a control is focused
findings.description: isTyping is computed only from tag==="INPUT" || tag==="TEXTAREA" || closest('.cm-editor') (lines 36-38). It does not account for native <select> elements or contentEditable regions. The app uses native focusable controls outside inputs (e.g. ToggleButtonGroup radios, custom dropdown buttons, listbox-style rows). While a <select> is open/focused, pressing Delete or Backspace falls through to the node/edge deletion branch (lines 174-191) and Ctrl+A falls through to select-all-nodes (lines 122-126) because none of these set isTyping. A user adjusting a focused control via keyboard can therefore unexpectedly delete selected nodes/edges or select every node. (Backspace on a focused button is the most reachable: it is not consumed by the button, so it reaches the window handler.)
findings.recommended_fix: Broaden the typing/focus guard: also treat tag==="SELECT", el.isContentEditable, and elements with role in {textbox,combobox,listbox,menu,menuitem,radio} (or any focused [contenteditable]) as 'isTyping' for the destructive shortcuts (Delete/Backspace, Ctrl+A, copy/paste). Centralising this in a small isEditableTarget(el) helper keeps the eight shortcut branches consistent.

findings.title: Heavy bottom-panel surfaces (OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, TracePanel) are eagerly imported into the initial entry chunk despite being conditionally rendered
findings.description: App.tsx statically imports OptimiserPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ModellingPreview, ExplorePreview and TracePanel at module top (lines 23-28). Each of these pulls in a large first-party subtree: the optimiser panel pulls FrontierChart, ConvergenceChart, SummaryTab, DetailCard, RatebookRatesTab, RatebookImpactBeeswarm, iterationSummary, ratebookFactorTables; ModellingPreview pulls 9 tab components (GLMCoefficientsTab, GLMRelativitiesTab, LossTab, LiftTab, ResidualsTab, FeaturesTab, AveTab, PdpTab, SummaryTab); TracePanel pulls StepCard, CalculationHero, WaterfallChart and the whole src/trace detail tree. Measured: the modelling + optimiser + trace source subtrees total 355,288 bytes of source, and all of it lands in the entry chunk. The built artifact confirms it: index-*.js is 440.3 KiB raw / 114.8 KiB gzip, and the gate reports initial total 237.4 KiB gzip against a 240 KiB budget -- only ~2.6 KiB of headroom. Yet every one of these panels is rendered conditionally (OptimiserPreview only when getOptimiserPreview(id) exists, ModellingPreview only when getModellingPreview(id) exists, OptimiserDataPreview only for optimiser nodes with preview data, ExplorePreview only for EXPLORE nodes, TracePanel only when traceResult is set). A user who opens the editor and never solves an optimiser, trains a model, or traces a cell downloads and parses all of this code for nothing. The codebase already has the exact mechanism to fix this: src/panels/LazyNodeEditors.tsx wraps config editors in React.lazy(() => import(...)) behind a LazyEditorBoundary Suspense, and NodePanel consumes them that way -- but the preview/trace surfaces were never migrated to it. Note the asymmetry: OptimiserConfig and ModellingConfig ARE lazy (separate 7.5 KiB / 9.8 KiB gzip chunks), while their heavier Preview siblings are eager. The charts are hand-rolled SVG (no d3/recharts/chart.js/plotly anywhere in src -- verified), so the win is purely from deferring first-party JS, with no vendor-dedup risk.
findings.recommended_fix: Add the five preview/trace panels to the existing lazy pattern. Either extend LazyNodeEditors.tsx (e.g. export const OptimiserPreview = lazy(() => import('./OptimiserPreview'))) or create a sibling LazyPreviewPanels.tsx, and wrap the conditional render blocks in App.tsx's DataPreview ErrorBoundary (and the TracePanel branch in the aside) in a <Suspense fallback={...}> with a lightweight panel-shaped skeleton. Because these only render after an async solve/train/trace completes, the chunk fetch is fully hidden behind work the user already waited for -- there is no perceptible loading penalty. This moves an estimated 60-90 KiB gzip out of the initial entry chunk, restoring real headroom under the 240 KiB budget.
findings.recommended_fix_note: Add the corresponding chunk-name prefixes (OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, TracePanel) to LAZY_ONLY_MODULEPRELOAD_CHUNK_PREFIXES in check-bundle-size.mjs so a future eager re-import is caught.

findings.title: Bundle-budget gate's lazy-only modulepreload check cannot detect a heavy panel becoming eager, and the lazy-only allowlist omits the preview/trace panels entirely
findings.description: The gate has two defenses against eager heavy code: (1) a 240 KiB initial-gzip ceiling, and (2) a LAZY_ONLY_MODULEPRELOAD_CHUNK_PREFIXES check that fails if a known lazy chunk appears as a startup <link rel=modulepreload>. Defense (2) is structurally blind to the most likely regression. When a developer adds a static import of a panel into App.tsx (as already happened for OptimiserPreview/ModellingPreview/TracePanel -- see the companion finding), Rollup MERGES that code into the index entry chunk; it does not emit a separate named chunk, so there is no 'OptimiserPreview-*.js' modulepreload link for the prefix check to flag. The chunk-name guard therefore only catches the narrow case of an already-split lazy chunk being preloaded, never the case of lazy code regressing back to eager. That leaves only defense (1), the size ceiling -- which the live build shows sitting at 237.4 / 240 KiB (~2.6 KiB / ~1% margin). A small future eager import will breach it, but the failure message ('Initial JS gzip size X exceeds budget') gives no hint about WHICH panel regressed, because they are all anonymized inside index-*.js. Compounding this, the allowlist itself omits the very surfaces that are currently eager and should be lazy: it lists CodeMirrorEditor, vendor-codemirror, vendor-layout, the editors, ModellingConfig and OptimiserConfig, but NOT OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview or TracePanel -- so even if those were split, the gate would not assert they stay lazy. The analyze:bundle sourcemap tooling exists but is a manual/opt-in script, not part of check:bundle, so it does not enforce per-source attribution in CI.
findings.recommended_fix: Strengthen the gate so eager-ness of heavy panels is detectable and enforced, not merely size-capped: (a) once the preview/trace panels are code-split (companion finding), add their chunk prefixes to LAZY_ONLY_MODULEPRELOAD_CHUNK_PREFIXES so any re-eager-ing surfaces as a build failure; (b) add a per-source assertion to check:bundle (reuse analyze-bundle-sourcemaps.mjs's contributor analysis) that fails if a source under src/panels/{optimiser,modelling}, src/trace, or the named preview files contributes generated bytes to the index entry chunk -- this catches eager merges that the modulepreload-name heuristic cannot; (c) consider tightening the initial budget back toward the documented ~200 KiB baseline once the panels are deferred, so the ~1% margin is restored to a meaningful operating buffer.
findings.recommended_fix_note: Defense (b) is the durable fix: it attributes entry-chunk bytes to source paths, so it is robust to chunk-name anonymization that defeats the prefix check.

results.note: Single biggest frontend-quality improvement: migrate the five conditionally-rendered bottom-panel surfaces (OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, TracePanel) off App.tsx's eager static imports and onto the codebase's existing React.lazy + LazyEditorBoundary Suspense pattern (already used for config editors in LazyNodeEditors.tsx). These panels carry ~355 KiB of first-party source (all hand-rolled SVG charts, no heavy vendor libs), are currently folded into the 440 KiB-raw / 114.8 KiB-gzip index entry chunk, and never render until an async solve/train/trace completes -- so deferring them hides the chunk fetch entirely behind work the user already awaited. This is the one change that both materially shrinks the initial download (the gate is at 237.4/240 KiB gzip, ~1% headroom) and closes the structural blind spot in the bundle gate, since the eager preview panels are the reason the 240 KiB ceiling is nearly exhausted in the first place. Both reuse code that already exists in the repo, so the engineering cost is low and the consistency benefit is high.

The single biggest frontend-quality improvement is making WebSocket disconnection a first-class, visible, and accessible state. This is a live file-sync editor: when the WS dies (server stopped, network drop, or retries exhausted after ~30s backoff x 50), the ONLY user-facing signal is a 2px colour-changed dot in the toolbar with a hover-only `title`. The dot is a decorative <span> (not focusable, no role/aria-live), so keyboard and screen-reader users get nothing, and even sighted users won't notice the editor has stopped receiving on-disk changes. Worse, in the terminal "disconnected" state there is no banner and no retry affordance (unlike the sessionExpired banner which offers a Reload button), so the user keeps editing against a silently-stale pipeline. Promote `disconnected`/`reconnecting` to an aria-live banner (mirroring the existing sessionExpired/syncBanner pattern in App.tsx:518-539) with a "Retry now" action that resets retriesRef and reconnects. This single change closes the highest-impact correctness-of-perception gap and the most severe accessibility gap simultaneously.

findings.location: frontend/src/components/Toolbar.tsx:90-94 (status dot); frontend/src/hooks/useWebSocketSync.ts:174-177, 95 (terminal disconnected state); frontend/src/App.tsx:517-539 (banner region where a disconnect banner is absent)
findings.title: WebSocket disconnect has no banner and no recovery affordance — live-sync silently dies behind a 2px dot
findings.description: useWebSocketSync drives three states (connected | reconnecting | disconnected). On terminal failure — connect() throwing (line 205), retries exhausted after MAX_RETRIES=50 with up to 30s backoff (lines 174-177), or never-opened abnormal close — status becomes 'disconnected'. The ONLY place this surfaces is the Toolbar status dot (Toolbar.tsx:90-94): a 2px <span> whose background colour changes to var(--danger) with a hover `title` of 'Server unreachable — restart haute serve'. There is no banner, no toast, and crucially no retry button. Contrast this with the two sibling failure states App.tsx already renders as full-width banners with actions: sessionExpired (App.tsx:518-531, with a Reload button) and syncBanner (App.tsx:533-539). For a tool whose entire premise is reflecting on-disk pipeline edits in real time, a dead socket means the canvas is now silently stale — the user keeps editing and saving against state that no longer round-trips, with zero prominent indication. Because the dot relies on colour + hover-title only, sighted users glancing at the canvas miss it, and (see separate a11y finding) keyboard/SR users cannot perceive it at all. After 50 retries the app also stops trying entirely, with no way to re-initiate a connection short of a full page reload.
findings.recommended_fix: Render a dismissible/persistent banner in the App.tsx main column (alongside sessionExpired/syncBanner) when wsStatus === 'disconnected' (and optionally a subtler one for prolonged 'reconnecting'). Give it role='alert', a clear message ('Live sync to the server was lost — file changes will not appear until reconnected'), and a 'Retry now' button that resets retriesRef.current=0 and re-runs connect() (expose a reconnect() callback from the hook, or key the effect off a manual retry counter). Keep the toolbar dot as a secondary indicator. This reuses the established banner pattern and removes the silent-stale-editor failure mode.

findings.title: Connection-status dot is colour-only and not exposed to assistive tech (no role/aria-live, hover-title only)
findings.description: The WS connection indicator is a bare <span className='w-2 h-2 rounded-full'> whose meaning is conveyed entirely by background colour (success/warning/danger) plus a `title` attribute. There is no `role`, no accessible name, and no aria-live region, so: (1) screen-reader users are never informed of connection state or of transitions to 'reconnecting'/'disconnected'; (2) the `title` tooltip is mouse-hover-only and not reachable by keyboard; (3) colour is the sole visual channel, failing WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Colour. The same colour-only pattern is used for the 'live' source dot (Toolbar.tsx:133-134, 158-160) and the dirty dot (line 89). Given this is the primary (and currently sole) signal that real-time sync is alive, its inaccessibility compounds the missing-banner issue above.
findings.recommended_fix: Make the indicator a focusable, labelled status element: add role='status' with an aria-live='polite' wrapper (or aria-label that updates with state, e.g. aria-label={wsConfig.title}), and pair the colour with a tiny glyph/text (e.g. a connected/alert icon) so state is not colour-only. At minimum give it an aria-label and ensure the state text is announced when it changes. Apply the same colour-plus-label treatment to the dirty and 'live source' dots.

findings.title: Preview error state is visual-only — backend/preview failures are not announced to screen readers
findings.description: When a node preview fails (status==='error'), DataPreview renders the error purely as an AlertCircle icon plus styled text inside a plain <div> (lines 280-286), and the header shows a second visual-only error chip (lines 416-421). Neither has role='alert' nor lives in an aria-live region, so a screen-reader user who triggers a preview and gets a backend error (timeout, contract error, Polars exception) receives no spoken feedback — the panel simply appears to do nothing. This is inconsistent with the codebase's own convention: NodePanel diagnostics (NodePanel.tsx:278, 516), InstanceReferenceDiagnostic, and Toast all correctly use role='alert'. The preview surface is the primary place users see execution failures, so it is the most important place to announce them.
findings.recommended_fix: Add role='alert' to the error container (DataPreview.tsx:280-286) so the failure message is announced when it appears. Consider also wrapping the status header region in an aria-live='polite' so status transitions (ok/error/loading) are conveyed. Ensure the error text is the accessible content (it already is plain text).

findings.title: Loading states ('Loading pipeline…', 'Executing pipeline…') are not announced — no role=status/aria-live
findings.description: The initial app load shows a centered 'Loading pipeline...' <div> (App.tsx:464-470) with no role='status' and no aria-live, so screen-reader users hear nothing while the pipeline loads and get no completion cue when the canvas appears. The same applies to DataPreview's in-flight states: the 'Executing pipeline...' overlay (DataPreview.tsx:276-279) and the header 'Running...' chip (lines 422-424) are animate-pulse text only. The project already knows the correct pattern — EditorLoadingFallback in LazyNodeEditors.tsx:25-34 uses role='status' aria-live='polite' aria-label='Loading editor' — but it is not applied to the two most prominent loading surfaces. Result: SR users cannot tell whether a long-running preview is working, stalled, or finished.
findings.recommended_fix: Add role='status' aria-live='polite' (with an aria-label such as 'Loading pipeline') to the App.tsx initial-load wrapper and to the DataPreview loading container, mirroring EditorLoadingFallback. This gives a spoken 'Loading…' on entry and an implicit completion cue when the region is replaced by content.

findings.title: Toasts use assertive role='alert' on every item inside a polite live-region container — conflicting/duplicated announcements
findings.description: Each ToastItem sets role='alert' (Toast.tsx:38), which carries an implicit aria-live='assertive', while the parent container also declares aria-live='polite' (Toast.tsx:66). This is contradictory: success and info toasts (e.g. 'Saved → file', 'Pipeline updated from file') are announced assertively, interrupting whatever the screen reader is currently saying, which is inappropriate for non-critical confirmations; and nesting an assertive live region inside a polite one yields undefined/duplicated announcement behaviour across AT. The information-severity is not differentiated — a routine 'success' interrupts the user the same way a hard 'error' does.
findings.recommended_fix: Differentiate by severity: use role='alert' (assertive) only for type==='error' (and possibly 'warning'); use role='status' (polite) for 'success'/'info'. Remove the redundant aria-live from one level — either keep a single polite live region on the container and drop per-item roles, or keep per-item roles and make the container a non-live wrapper. Ensure each toast is announced exactly once.

findings.location: frontend/src/panels/PanelShell.tsx:5-24 (fixed MIN_PANEL_W=320, px math); frontend/src/index.css (0 @media queries); frontend/src/App.tsx:498-714 (fixed horizontal flex layout)
findings.title: No responsive breakpoints anywhere — fixed-px three-column layout breaks on narrow/zoomed viewports
findings.description: The entire frontend contains zero @media queries (grep across src/*.css and *.tsx returns none) and no container-query usage. The shell is a fixed horizontal flex: left palette (LEFT_PALETTE_W=180 / collapsed 40, PanelShell.tsx:6-7), a flex-1 canvas+preview centre, and a right panel whose minimum is MIN_PANEL_W=320 (PanelShell.tsx:5). On a narrow window (or high browser zoom / split-screen), the right panel cannot shrink below 320px and the palette consumes another 40-180px, so the canvas centre is squeezed and the toolbar's many fixed-width controls (Toolbar.tsx) overflow with no wrapping or stacking. Nothing collapses, stacks, or switches to an overlay below a threshold. DataPreview does have internal width tiers (responsiveColumnWidth, DataPreview.tsx:87-91) but the overall page chrome does not adapt. index.html does set a proper viewport meta, so the app advertises responsiveness it doesn't implement. This is a desktop-class tool so the severity is low, but at staff-quality bar the layout should degrade gracefully rather than overflow.
findings.recommended_fix: Introduce at least one breakpoint: below ~900px collapse the left palette to its icon rail by default and reduce/await MIN_PANEL_W (or convert the right panel to a slide-over overlay rather than an in-flow column). Allow the toolbar control cluster to wrap or move secondary controls into an overflow menu under a width threshold. Even a single 'compact' breakpoint that prevents horizontal overflow would close the gap.

findings.location: frontend/src/App.tsx:24-26 (eager imports of OptimiserPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ModellingPreview, ExplorePreview)
findings.title: Heavy result-preview panels are eagerly imported into App while config editors are lazy — inconsistent splitting, larger initial bundle
findings.description: App.tsx statically imports OptimiserPreview (824 lines, pulling its whole optimiser/ chart subtree: FrontierChart, ConvergenceChart, SummaryTab, RatebookRatesTab, DetailCard, RatebookImpactBeeswarm), OptimiserDataPreview (768 lines), ExplorePreview (260 lines), and ModellingPreview — all into the initial bundle (App.tsx:23-26). These panels render only conditionally (App.tsx:589-637) when a user opens an optimiser/modelling/explore result, which is a minority of sessions. Meanwhile every NodePanel config editor IS code-split via React.lazy (LazyNodeEditors.tsx:3-23) and elkjs is dynamically imported (utils/layout.ts:14-19), so the project clearly adopts lazy-loading as a pattern — but the largest result-preview surfaces bypass it and load up front for all users. (Note: no recharts/d3 dependency — charts are custom SVG — so this is bundle weight from app code, not a third-party chart lib.)
findings.recommended_fix: Wrap OptimiserPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, and ModellingPreview in React.lazy with a Suspense fallback (reuse the existing LazyEditorBoundary or a small skeleton), matching the NodePanel editor pattern, so their chunks load only when a result of that type is actually displayed. This trims the initial JS for the common edit-only session.
